subject: Accounting
title: The Role of Corporate Governance
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Role of Corporate Governance.

hook.text: Enron's board had a finance committee, an audit committee, and a code of ethics. None stopped the fraud.

buildup.text: Corporate governance means the systems that oversee management and protect shareholders.

discovery.text: Strong boards have independent directors who ask hard questions and hold executives accountable.

twist.text: After Enron, many companies added truly independent directors—but rubber-stamp boards still exist.

climax.text: Good governance alone can't prevent fraud, but weak governance almost guarantees it will go unchecked.

punchline.text: Governance is a lock, not a guarantee.

quiz.question: What is corporate governance designed to do?
options: Maximize stock price at all costs

details.summary: Corporate governance—the system of rules, practices, and processes by which companies are directed and controlled—failed spectacularly in every major accounting scandal. This topic examines how weak boards, absent oversight, and conflicts of interest enable fraud.
details.whyItMatters: Strong corporate governance is the primary defense against fraud. When boards fail to exercise genuine oversight, management is free to manipulate accounting without accountability.
takeaways: Independent boards with empowered audit committees are the strongest fraud deterrents
Scandals repeatedly feature boards dominated by insiders who rubber-stamp management decisions
Post-scandal reforms focused heavily on board independence, audit committee expertise, and executive accountability

faq.question: How does corporate governance prevent accounting fraud?
faq.answer: Effective governance puts independent directors on the board, empowers audit committees with financial expertise, separates the CEO and chairman roles, protects whistleblowers, and ensures the external auditor reports to the board—not management.

faq.question: What governance failures were common across major scandals?
faq.answer: Common failures include boards dominated by insiders or friends of the CEO, audit committees lacking financial expertise, external auditors reporting to management rather than the board, no whistleblower protections, and excessive executive compensation tied to short-term stock performance.
